title: After a construction contract grew by a quarter: the next contracts
question: When a builder's contract grew by a quarter or more, or closed well over the original, did the same department award it new construction contracts, and did builders that finished near the original fare any differently?
finding: 23 builder-and-department pairs had a construction contract that rose a quarter or more above its first figure at least a year ago. 10 of them (43%) were awarded new construction contracts by the same department afterwards: 42 contracts with ceilings of $308.1 million. Of 32 pairs whose contract was closed out with no commission-approved increase on file, 16 (50%) were awarded new contracts afterwards. A gap that size in favour of the builders that finished near the original would arise by chance 42% of the time; in favour of those that grew, 77%. The most new work followed Esquivel Grading & Paving Inc (Public Works; 6th Street Pedestrian Safety Project (1000015023) rose +30%): 13 new contracts, $97.5 million. Construction contracts above a threshold go to the lowest responsive bid under the Administrative Code, and the Controller's 2014 audit found that past performance is not considered in the award. Nothing in these records shows a builder shut out, or favoured, after a contract grew.
how: The commissions that oversee construction (Public Utilities, Airport, Port, Public Works since late 2022, and the transit Board) vote on contract changes above what staff may approve, and on close-outs; those items were read into one record per contract number and department. The first figure is the original amount where an item prints it (or, for the Public Utilities Commission, the award in its minutes); otherwise it is the amount that stood before the first change on file, which already includes earlier staff-approved changes and so understates growth. The latest figure is the final amount at close-out, or the total in the latest item. Where the Board of Supervisors approved the same change as a commission, the commission's row is kept and the Board's dropped; where a numbered modification appears twice, the later row is kept. Design-build and construction-manager contracts, which grow as phases and work packages are added, and professional-services contracts are kept apart from fixed-price construction. A pair is listed when one of the builder's fixed-price construction contracts in the department stands a quarter or more above its first figure; the date is that of the item that took it past a quarter (or the close-out). New contracts are construction contracts in the Supplier Contracts table for the same builder and department that began after that date, leaving out the grown contract itself. Bid sheets entered and won afterwards are counted from the published tabulations already read for the low-bid screen (Public Works, Port and the transit agency only). The comparison group is builders whose contract was closed out by a commission with no commission-approved price increase on file and, where it can be measured, less than 10% above the first figure; pairs need a year of follow-up and a name found in the contract table.
limits: Amounts and days are copied from agenda items and minutes and parsed from their wording; contractor names are phrases from the item text. A total in an item is an authorization, often including contingency, not money paid. Most Public Works rows are agenda items as proposed, because minutes before 2025 are not posted. A contract appears in these files only when a change needed a commission vote, so small changes approved by staff are invisible, and departments set that line differently: rates can be compared within a department, not across. Change orders for conditions found underground and for work the owner adds are an ordinary part of construction. Winning the next low-bid contract is what the law provides for, whatever happened on the last one; the comparison group is small and comes mostly from one department (Public Utilities, the only one that publishes close-outs as commission items). A builder with no new contract may simply not have bid. What would settle whether performance is weighed at all is the contractor evaluation record, which the Budget and Legislative Analyst found barely used.
